title: Nasdaq's 5.3% October Swoon: AI Capex Fears Meet a History of 24% Rebound Years
text:
Nasdaq's 5.3% October Swoon: AI Capex Fears Meet a History of 24% Rebound Years — BigGo Finance Ask AI Real-time News Market Earnings Call Event Calendar Watchlist Podcast Market Influencers Earnings Call Event Calendar Watchlist Podcast Market Influencers More Ask AI Real-time News Watchlist Holdings Market Earnings Call Event Calendar Podcast Market Influencers Nasdaq's 5.3% October Swoon: AI Capex Fears Meet a History of 24% Rebound Years
 Add preferred source 2 The Nasdaq Composite's 5.3% October decline, driven by investor unease over massive AI capital spending at Alphabet, Amazon and their peers, has revived a historical pattern: after the prior 14 monthly drops of 5% or more over the past decade, the index gained an average of 24% over the following year. Hyperscaler capex is projected to approach $900 billion in 2026, and negative free cash flow at major technology companies has rattled shareholders. Leveraged funds amplified the selloff, with SOXL tumbling 24.75% in a single session and rebalancing sales estimated above $40 billion. Morgan Stanley sees the correction 80% to 90% complete and points to the midterm elections, AI financing absorption and easier liquidity as catalysts, while warning that further declines are possible. Key Elements 
 Nasdaq Composite JPMorgan Chase Alphabet Amazon Intel SOXL Morgan Stanley Mike Wilson Dubravko Lakos-Bujas Invesco QQQ Trust Nasdaq-100 Microsoft OpenAI Anthropic CoreWeave Nikkei 225 Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group Steno Research The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.3% in October, its steepest monthly decline since early 2025, as investors recoiled from the capital-spending bills piling up across the largest technology companies. The drop has revived a question that has shadowed the artificial intelligence trade all year: when does all that spending start producing cash?
 History offers one answer, and it is a bullish one. Over the past decade, the index has posted 15 monthly losses of 5% or more, including October, and in the 12 months following the prior 14 episodes it gained an average of 24%, according to YCharts data cited in a Motley Fool analysis. The record is uneven. The aftermath of the February 2020 selloff brought a 52% gain, and March 2020 was followed by a 72% advance. But the 2022 drawdowns produced losses, including a 27% decline after September 2021 and a 19% drop after January 2022.

 The selling was concentrated in the companies footing the AI bill. Capital expenditure across the five largest hyperscalers topped $400 billion in 2025 and is now projected to approach $900 billion in 2026, up from an earlier forecast of $736 billion, according to JPMorgan Chase. The bank expects global AI capital spending to exceed $5.5 trillion by 2030.
 Alphabet and Amazon both reported negative free cash flow for the quarter, and shareholders punished them for it. Alphabet lost roughly $500 billion in market value in a single session, and Amazon's trailing 12-month free cash flow deficit widened to $42.4 billion from $7.6 billion in the second quarter. Intel compounded the damage, warning of soft PC demand amid memory shortages and server processor constraints tied to advanced substrate supply, and its shares fell 28.6% in a day, the largest drop on record for the chipmaker.
 JPMorgan market strategist Dubravko Lakos-Bujas argued that the market has swung too far. "The Street appears to be underwriting the AI data center monetization case: Elevated capex today should ultimately translate into higher revenue, stronger margins, and expanding cash flow," he said.
 The operating results themselves did little to support the case that AI demand is fading. Google Cloud revenue grew 103%, Microsoft's Azure rose 48%, and Amazon Web Services expanded 39%, its fastest pace in five years. AWS said a substantial share of capacity through 2028 is already booked and guided to growth above 40% in both 2027 and 2028, well ahead of consensus estimates of 35% and 30%.
 Microsoft Chief Executive Satya Nadella told investors he has rarely been more confident about the returns on the company's long-term investment, pointing to demand, product competitiveness and efficiency gains.

 The gap between spending and collection is the crux of the debate. Facilities must be built and powered before customers pay, and the larger the buildout, the more financing it requires. Microsoft, the only one of the group still generating positive free cash flow, saw its free cash flow fall 27% over the past year. Signs of tightening capital are appearing elsewhere: OpenAI cut its fundraising target to $20 billion from $30 billion and its valuation goal to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion after some investors reduced commitments, according to the Financial Times, while Blackstone told investors it expects Anthropic to carry a credit rating in the BB range after listing, below its earlier expectation of investment grade by 2027.
 The pressure has been most visible in the debt of the companies that build AI capacity, rather than in the hyperscalers that buy it. CoreWeave's 9.625% unsecured notes due in 2032 fell below 80 cents on the dollar on Oct. 14, lifting the yield above 15%, and its five-year credit default swaps touched 1,194.5 basis points on Oct. 15, a level that implies a better-than-even chance of default within five years, according to ICE data. Global AI-related debt issuance fell to $23 billion in September from a record $113 billion in June, Morgan Stanley data show, though this year's total of about $466 billion is still more than four times the $101 billion raised in the same period of 2025.
 The repricing crossed the Pacific. On Oct. 15 the Nikkei 225 fell 4.9%, or 3,318.34 points, to 64,425.95, its third-largest point decline on record, as AI and semiconductor shares led a sixth straight session of losses, Reuters reported. Japanese banks are also part of the funding chain: Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group was a co-structuring agent and joint bookrunner on CoreWeave's $8.5 billion DDTL 4.0 facility alongside Morgan Stanley, a deal CoreWeave described as the first investment-grade-rated financing secured by high-performance computing infrastructure.
 Leveraged products amplified the move. SOXL, a fund that tracks three times the daily return of the semiconductor index, drew a record $7 billion this month, according to Bloomberg, and plunged 24.75% on Oct. 30 alone. On that day the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 7.2%, the Nasdaq dropped 2.86% and the S&P 500 lost 1.82%. Leveraged funds must rebalance daily, and estimates put end-of-day selling tied to those adjustments above $40 billion, including $19.2 billion linked to semiconductor exposure and $14.6 billion tied to the Nasdaq-100.
 Hedge funds had already been cutting risk. Client data compiled by JPMorgan showed hedge funds down 3.3% for the month through the prior week, with long-short performance the weakest since early 2021. Gross exposure among equity long-short funds had fallen 7.8% from its peak as of Oct. 27, the largest reduction since Steno Research began tracking the data in 2016. An equal-weighted S&P 500 exchange-traded fund slipped just 0.8% that day and is up nearly 5% for October, a sign that the damage reflected crowded positioning more than a broad collapse in valuations.
 Bank of America chief investment strategist Michael Hartnett described the technology selloff as "typical tightening pain" that would not prove fatal absent job losses or a credit-market crisis.
 Morgan Stanley Chief Investment Officer Mike Wilson said in an Oct. 27 interview, before Alphabet reported, that the correction that began in June was 80% to 90% complete, though he stopped short of calling a bottom. He warned the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index could fall another 10% to 15% by mid-November and put S&P 500 support at 7,100 to 7,200, below the Oct. 30 close of 7,580.07. The firm has kept its year-end S&P 500 target of 8,000.
 Wilson identified three potential catalysts for a rebound: the conclusion of the midterm elections on Nov. 3, absorption of the remaining AI-related debt and equity issuance, and a signal of easier liquidity from the Federal Reserve or the Treasury. He compared the setup to 2018, when the S&P 500 fell nearly 15% more between the midterms and Christmas Eve before rallying in January as the Fed turned cautious. Meta's $22.5 billion common stock offering, which drew five times oversubscription and was upsized 10%, offers a recent example of the market absorbing supply.
 Historical election patterns support the bullish case. BlackRock data show the S&P 500 has returned an average of 14.1% in the six months after midterm elections since 1970, more than double the 5.7% average in non-election years. Citadel Securities' Scott Rubner said most institutional clients view the vote as a clearing event and have held off on buying until it passes.
 Geopolitics cuts the other way. The Wall Street Journal reported that the U.S. has told Gulf states to prepare for a short, intense military operation after the election, and Brent crude approached this year's high of $117.60 a barrel on Oct. 30 after a tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz. A renewed climb in oil would revive inflation concerns and tighten financing conditions for AI builders.
 In Seoul, DS Investment & Securities strategist Yang Hyung-mo called November "a buying month," citing easing domestic margin debt and stable U.S. rates, while cautioning that further declines remain possible given memory prices that could erode demand and the risk of renewed strikes on Iran after the vote.
 For investors, the tension is between a historical base rate that favors buying dips and a financing cycle that has not yet fully played out. The average 24% gain that followed past 5% monthly declines is a statistic, not a guarantee, and the 2022 episodes show how long the recovery can take when the drawdown coincides with a tightening cycle. What the next few weeks will test is whether the selling was mostly a positioning unwind, as the equal-weight index suggests, or the start of a repricing of AI spending that has yet to earn its return.
